summary: Arabic has no separate words for “my, your, his …”: a suffix goes on the noun. كِتَابِي my book, كِتَابُكَ your book (to a man), كِتَابُكِ (to a woman), كِتَابُهُ his book, كِتَابُهَا her book, كِتَابُنَا our book, كِتَابُكُمْ your book (several), كِتَابُهُمْ their book (for women only: -kunna, -hunna). The suffix makes the noun definite: no article, no tanwīn. The case vowel stays in front of the suffix (كِتَابُكَ subject, كِتَابَكَ object, كِتَابِكَ after a preposition) — only -ī swallows it. A final ة becomes t: غُرْفَتِي. أَب and أَخ lengthen: أَبُوكَ (your father), أَخُوهُ (his brother) — but أَبِي, أَخِي. A dual loses its -ni: وَالِدَايَ (my parents). In “X of Y” the suffix goes on the last noun: اِبْنُ عَمِّي (my cousin).

blocks.caption: These are the subject (nominative) forms. The same suffixes go on prepositions: عِنْدِي (I have), عِنْدَكَ, عِنْدَهُ …

blocks.title: A noun with a suffix is definite.
blocks.text: Never add the article: كِتَابِي, not *الْكِتَابِي; and no tanwīn: كِتَابُهُ, not *كِتَابٌهُ. That is why هٰذَا كِتَابِي is a sentence: “this is my book”.

blocks.title: ة → ت, and the special nouns أَب / أَخ.
blocks.text: Before any suffix the tāʾ marbūṭa is written and said ت: أُسْرَتِي, زَوْجَتُهُ, خَالَتُكِ. أَب and أَخ add a long vowel that shows the case: أَبُوكَ (nom.), أَبَاكَ (acc.), أَبِيكَ (gen.) — but “my father” is أَبِي in every case.

blocks.title: -hu and -hum after i.
blocks.text: After i or y the suffixes -hu / -hum become -hi / -him: فِي بَيْتِهِ (in his house), عَلَيْهِمْ (on them). You will meet it after prepositions (lesson 11).

“my …”
blocks.caption: Arabic has no single word for cousin, nephew or niece: it always says whose child. The first noun is in the construct form (اِبْنُ — no article, no tanwīn) and the suffix goes on the last one.

blocks.text: Dual and plural nouns take the suffixes too: وَالِدَايَ (my parents — the dual without -ni), أَجْدَادِي (my grandparents), إِخْوَتِي (my brothers). A sound masculine plural drops its -na: مُعَلِّمُوكَ (your teachers).

askYourself: Does the noun end in ة? → t before the suffix: غُرْفَتِي.
Remove the article and the tanwīn — the suffix already makes the noun definite.
Which case is the noun in? Keep -u / -a / -i before the suffix (not before -ī).
Is it أَب or أَخ? → أَبُو- / أَخُو- (nominative) before every suffix except -ī.
Is it “my cousin / nephew”? → construct + the suffix on the last noun: اِبْنُ عَمِّي.

traps: *الْكِتَابِي — never the article with a suffix.
*أَبُكَ — “your father” is أَبُوكَ; “my father” is أَبِي.
“My parents” is وَالِدَايَ: the dual loses its -ni.
To a man -ka, to a woman -ki: unvocalized كتابك can be either.
In “my uncle's son” the suffix is on “uncle”: اِبْنُ عَمِّي, not *اِبْنِي عَمٍّ.

quiz.why: ة → t before the suffix, and no article.

quiz.why: أَب lengthens: أَبُو- in the nominative.
The dual drops -ni before the suffix: wālidā + ya.
In “X of Y” the suffix goes on the last noun; the first is in the construct form.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has both: a separate word, הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי (everyday), and suffixes cognate with the Arabic ones, סִפְרִי (formal) — compare كِتَابِي.
German uses separate words that decline like ein: mein Bruder, meine Schwester, unser Haus.
Chinese puts 的 after the owner: 我的书; with close family the 的 is often left out: 我妈妈.
The same suffixes on عِنْدَ give “to have”: عِنْدِي (at me = I have).
